title: Unlocking Teacher Development: CPD Session Checklist
author: Adam Robbins
summary: Adam Robbins shares a checklist he has developed for planning CPD sessions after two years focused on thinking about professional development rather than blogging, built around what he's seen go wrong when sessions miss the EEF's mechanisms for effective CPD. The checklist runs from a 'Do Now' recall activity, through explicitly justifying the session with 'Why this?' and 'Why now?' framing tied to the school improvement plan, into a 'Setting the scene' step naming the persistent problem the session solves. The explaining phase follows an 'explain, evidence, then define' sequence with two worked examples, a deliberate non-example showing common misapplication, and a discussion prompt. Practice includes deliberate rehearsal (teacher-led, then in trios) and scenario-based checks using fictitious teachers applying the technique correctly and incorrectly. The session closes with reflection, public commitment to specific lesson contexts, and collaborative co-planning so teachers leave 'next lesson ready.' Robbins illustrates every step with a worked example on introducing choral response as the CPD topic itself.
points: Robbins's 'Why this? Why now?' opening step forces CPD leaders to justify both the topic's value and its timing against the school improvement plan before any technique is taught -- a structural safeguard against CPD that feels arbitrary to attending teachers.

The 'explain, evidence, then define' sequence (borrowed from Adam Boxer) deliberately delays naming the technique until after its rationale and evidence base have been established, so teachers understand why before they learn what to call it.

The deliberate 'non-example' step -- showing a common misapplication of the technique being taught -- gives teachers a specific error pattern to recognize and avoid, not just a correct model to imitate.

Ending with co-planning (adapting curriculum resources collaboratively so teachers leave 'next lesson ready') targets the common CPD failure mode where a session ends with intent to change practice but no concrete artifact ready for the next lesson.
quotes: Over the last two years I have spent a lot less time blogging and a lot more time thinking about CPD.
I've noticed that often when CPD goes bad it misses many of the EEF's mechanisms for effective CPD.
Explain the solution to the problem, citing evidence from relevant sources, before naming the technique and clearly defining it.
I say you say: Photosynthesis is when plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water
Any routine that is introduced will need practicing. Firstly, with you leading, then in trios.
How does this new technique fit into my subject/stage etc. Leaders publicly commit to how their team will begin using this technique.
